events.description: Al-Shamrani's shooting at NAS Pensacola killed three US sailors and wounded eight.
Al-Shamrani posted 'the countdown has begun' while visiting the 9/11 Memorial.
AQAP emir Qasim al-Rimi was killed in a US drone strike in Yemen, a few weeks before the early Feb video.
AQAP video claimed 'full responsibility' for Pensacola and described al-Shamrani as a sleeper agent.
DOJ and FBI press conference announcing access to al-Shamrani's phones and criticizing Apple.
Shooting at NAS Corpus Christi by Adam Alsahli; a sailor survived and a barrier was closed.
US-Taliban agreement signed in Doha; no formal Taliban renunciation of al-Qaeda; al-Qaeda issued a statement supporting it.
US officials drafted a renunciation-of-terrorism statement in Mullah Omar's name for the Taliban's Doha office to read; it was never read.
Hibatullah Akhundzada issued an Eid al-Fitr statement calling for an Islamic system and offering amnesty.
Taliban issued a religious decree (fatwa) stating the only acceptable outcome is reestablishing the Islamic Emirate with Hibatullah as emir.
Hibatullah's son reportedly carried out a suicide bombing in Gereshk district, Helmand.
Charlie Hebdo attack, facilitated and executed by AQAP.
ISIS attacks in Paris on stadiums, the Bataclan and restaurants.
San Bernardino terrorist attack; Apple refused to break the security of the attackers' iPhone.
US-Taliban withdrawal agreement signed; hosts say there is no hint of a Taliban break with al-Qaeda since then.
Taliban statement dismissing power-sharing as a 'silly ministerial post'.
Taliban statement after the withdrawal agreement offering a general amnesty to opponents.

key_claims: AQAP's claim that al-Shamrani was its sleeper agent was borne out by the FBI's phone access, which showed he communicated with AQAP operatives until the night before the attack.
Abdullah al-Maliki was an obscure AQAP external operations figure in Yemen who communicated with al-Shamrani and was targeted after Pensacola.
Qasim al-Rimi, a veteran who joined al-Qaeda in the 1990s and helped relaunch AQAP in 2009, was killed in early 2020, which shows AQAP's resilience.
The hosts argue that al-Qaeda's leadership had a stand-down order on large Western attacks, and that its capacity and decision to attempt one remain open questions, especially with the US withdrawal.
There is no evidence of any Taliban break with al-Qaeda since the Feb 29, 2020 deal; the Taliban has made zero attacks on al-Qaeda and AQIS fighters remain unhanded.
The US is suppressing enemy-initiated attack, airstrike and district-control data that show the Taliban on the offensive against Afghan forces.
Hibatullah's Eid statement offers 'no monopoly' on power but only under Taliban-enforced Sharia and amnesty for opponents, which the hosts take as incompatible with power-sharing.
The hosts say the Afghan government can no longer rely on the Trump administration and should seek other allies.
The hosts argue the Taliban still seeks to restore a monopoly Islamic Emirate under Hibatullah Akhundzada rather than share power with the Afghan government.
The hosts say there is no evidence of a Taliban break with al-Qaeda since the 29 Feb 2020 agreement, and al-Qaeda endorses the Taliban's Islamic Emirate.
The hosts read the Taliban's 'divine Sharia law' language as consistent with al-Qaeda's radical beliefs.
The hosts argue the Taliban's amnesty offers signal they expect to defeat opponents, not to share power.
The hosts criticize General Miller as either a fool or willingly duped over Taliban promises to reduce violence.
